docs.title: SPARC
docs.text:
Shapley Pareto Robust Concept attribution with fuzzy logic. Post hoc explanations of tabular black box models that are stable, calibrated and sparse.

Charis Ntakolia, Department of Aeronautical Studies, Hellenic Air Force Academy.

pip install "sparc-xai[plots]"

SPARC attributes a prediction to fuzzy concepts of correlated features instead of to single features, so that the credit of a prediction is not split arbitrarily among features that carry the same information. Every attribution is estimated over bootstrap resamples and several model classes and reported as a trapezoidal fuzzy number with a sign confidence, a disagreement index between model classes and a linguistic label such as weakly positive. The number of concepts, the fuzzifier, the sparsity and the alpha level are selected from a Pareto front that trades off fidelity loss, complexity and instability; a knee point is reported by default and the whole front is kept, so that the sparse default and the most faithful explanation are both one call away.

docs.title: Estimator options
docs.text: The constructor of sparc.Explainer exposes the design choices of the method. The defaults follow the ablation analysis of the study; the options below are the ones worth knowing.

docs.title: The pool
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning model_classes gradient boosting, random forest, multilayer perceptron The model classes of the pool; the first is the reference model whose output is explained. Pass [("name", estimator), ...]. n_resamples 50 Bootstrap resamples B; resample 0 is the original data. background_size 100 Background sample of the Shapley computation, drawn from the training rows of every pool member. explainer "auto" "tree", "linear", "exact", "permutation" or "kernel"; "auto" picks the exact tree estimator for tree ensembles, the exact estimator up to ten features and permutation sampling above. task, target_class "auto", 1 Regression or classification, and the class whose probability is explained.

The pool over model classes is what makes the intervals honest: in the ablation study a single model class kept the stability but lost the calibration of the intervals (support coverage fell from 0.92 to 0.99 down to 0.78 to 0.95 across datasets).

docs.title: The concepts
docs.text: Option Default Meaning n_concepts_grid, fuzzifier_grid 2 to 6, 1.5 to 2.5 Candidate numbers of concepts and fuzzifiers of fuzzy c means. concept_distance "correlation" Features are clustered by their correlation profiles; "loading" uses factor loadings instead. consensus False Consensus clustering over resamples of the instances, more stable partitions at a cost. apriori_groups, partition_source None, "both" A known grouping of the features as a candidate partition; "data", "apriori" or "both". crisp_concepts False Ablation: harden the partitions. Crisp concepts keep the stability, and in the ablation they removed the output faster on one dataset because fuzzy removal is partial.

docs.title: The fuzzy numbers
docs.text: Option Default Meaning fuzzy_shape "trapezoidal" Or "triangular". support_percentiles, core_percentiles (5, 95), (25, 75) The quantiles of the pool that form the support and the core. disagreement_threshold 0.5 Above this disagreement index an attribution is upgraded to an interval type 2 number, one trapezoid per model class. linguistic_labels, linguistic_scale five labels, "mean_abs" The label set and the standardization of the attribution axis.

docs.title: The selection
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning alpha_grid, sparsity_grid 0 to 1 in steps of 0.25, 1 to K Alpha levels of the cut and numbers of retained concepts evaluated. solver "grid" Exhaustive evaluation; "nsga2" for large decision spaces; "fixed" evaluates fixed_configuration only (ablation). knee_method "utopia" The default explanation: the front member closest to the utopia point; "hyperplane" is the alternative. surrogate, cv "linear", 5 The surrogate and the folds of the fidelity loss.

The selection is what buys stability and sparsity: without it (five concepts, all retained) the surrogate fit is perfect and the insertion area higher, but the deletion area is much worse and the rank stability falls to 0.46 to 0.75. The price of the knee is a lower insertion area, which is why the front, the fidelity optimal member and explanation.at() are part of the interface.

docs.title: The point estimate and the estimator
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning point_estimate "reference" The reported number is the attribution of the reference model on the original data, while the fuzzy number, the sign confidence and the disagreement describe the whole pool. "centroid" reports the centroid of the trapezoid instead. concept_estimator "aggregate" The concept attribution is the membership weighted sum of feature level Shapley values. "direct" computes Shapley values over the fuzzy concepts of the selected partition directly (sparc.concept_shapley): every concept is a player and a coalition keeps features to the degree of their membership. direct_imputation "conditional" How the direct estimator removes features: by the mean of the nearest background rows on the kept features, or "marginal", the mean over the background sample. feature_weights "membership" How a concept's credit is redistributed to its features by feature_attribution; "importance" weights the members by their mean absolute feature level attribution.

What the ablation found. The reference centred point raises the fit of the reported attribution to the model on every dataset (surrogate R² from 0.87 to 0.97 on one of them) and changes nothing else, hence the default. The direct estimator with marginal imputation reproduces the aggregated one within 0.01 on every metric: the interventional concept game and the membership aggregation of interventional feature values agree, which is a useful check of the method's foundation. The direct estimator with conditional imputation anticipates the removal used by deletion tests and improves the deletion area on some datasets, but it pays with rank stability, so it is an option and an ablation, not the default.

docs.text: Blue is a positive attribution, orange a negative one. Thin lines are supports (the central 90 percent of the pool by default), thick lines cores (the central 50 percent). Colour scales for concept scores run from blue (low) to red (high).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "sparc-xai[plots]"

Python 3.10 or later. The package is imported as sparc. Without the plots extra everything works except sparc.plots.

docs.title: Fit, explain, read
docs.text:
import sparc
from sparc.synthetic import make_synthetic
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

problem = make_synthetic("additive", n_samples=800, n_features=9, rho=0.8, n_factors=3, random_state=0)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(problem.X, problem.y, random_state=0)

explainer = sparc.Explainer(n_resamples=20, random_state=0)
explainer.fit(X_train, y_train, feature_names=[f"x{j}" for j in range(9)])
explanation = explainer(X_test[:50])

print(explanation)
print(explanation.describe(0))

Explainer.fit trains the pool: every model class on the original data and on n_resamples - 1 bootstrap resamples. The default model classes are a gradient boosting model, which is the reference model, a random forest and a multilayer perceptron; a classifier is explained through the probability of target_class. fit also forms the candidate concept partitions by fuzzy c means on the correlation profiles of the features, for every number of concepts in n_concepts_grid and every fuzzifier in fuzzifier_grid.

explainer(X) computes the feature level Shapley values of every pool member for the instances of X, aggregates them to every candidate partition, evaluates every configuration (partition, sparsity, alpha level) on the three objectives, keeps the Pareto front and returns the explanation at the knee.

The sentence form of one instance reads like this:

Instance 0: model output 0.773
Configuration: K=3, fuzzifier=2.0, sparsity=2, alpha=0.00
  C2 (x3, x4, x5): weakly positive (compatibility 1.00), centroid +1.05, support [+0.79, +1.32], core [+0.9, +1.15], sign confidence 1.00, ...
  C1 (x0, x1, x2): negligible (compatibility 0.90), centroid +0.273, support [-0.33, +0.86], ...

docs.text:
from sparc import plots

plots.bar(explanation)                  # concept importance with the support of the fuzzy global importance
plots.interval_bars(explanation[0])     # one instance: point, core, support, sign confidence, disagreement
plots.front(explanation)                # the Pareto front with the knee and the fidelity optimal member

docs.title: Your own models
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor, ExtraTreesRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor

explainer = sparc.Explainer(model_classes=[
    ("hgb", HistGradientBoostingRegressor()),     # the first is the reference model
    ("et", ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=200)),
    ("mlp", MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 64), max_iter=500)),
])

Any scikit-learn estimator with fit and predict (or predict_proba) works; tree ensembles are explained exactly and fast, other models through the exact or the permutation estimator depending on the number of features. Known groups of features enter as a candidate partition with apriori_groups={"group name": [column indices or names], ...} and partition_source="both".

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The concept attribution of SPARC satisfies four properties that feature level attributions do not have, or do not have at the concept level. Each is checked numerically in tests/test_properties.py and tests/test_concept_shapley.py.

Efficiency at the concept level. For every membership matrix whose rows sum to one, the concept attributions of an instance sum to the model output minus the expected output over the background sample:

\[\sum_{k=1}^{K} \phi_k(x) = f(x) - \mathbb{E}[f], \qquad \phi_k(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} u_{jk}\,\varphi_j(x),\]

where \(\varphi_j\) is the feature level Shapley value and \(u_{jk}\) the membership of feature \(j\) in concept \(k\). With the reference centred point estimate values.sum(axis=1) + base_values equals output exactly.

Reduction. With the identity partition (one crisp concept per feature), one resample and one model class the method returns the feature level Shapley values exactly, and the fuzzy numbers degenerate to points.

Symmetry. Two concepts whose aggregated contributions coincide in every coalition receive the same attribution, inherited from the symmetry of the Shapley value applied to every pool member.

Duplication invariance. Adding an exact copy of a feature leaves the attribution of the concept that absorbs the copy unchanged, whereas the feature level attribution of the copied feature is split between the copies.

docs.title: The concept game
docs.text:
The direct estimator (concept_estimator="direct") shows where these properties come from. Let every concept be a player of a cooperative game. A coalition \(S\) of concepts keeps feature \(j\) to the degree

\[w_j(S) = \min\Big(1, \sum_{k \in S} u_{jk}\Big),\]

the membership mass of \(j\) in \(S\); the grand coalition keeps every feature and the empty coalition removes every feature. The value of a coalition is the model output with the remaining features removed to the degree \(1 - w_j(S)\), by marginal imputation (the interventional expectation over the background) or by conditional imputation. The Shapley value of concept \(k\) in this game is the direct concept attribution. With marginal imputation it coincides with the membership aggregation of the interventional feature level values in practice, so the aggregation of Equation 1 is the Shapley value of a game over fuzzy concepts, not only a convenient sum. With crisp concepts the game is the grouped Shapley value, with the identity partition the feature level Shapley value; both reductions are tested exactly.

docs.title: Calibration and stability
docs.text: Two further properties are empirical rather than axiomatic and are the subject of the study: the support and the core of the fuzzy numbers cover an independent replicate attribution at about their nominal levels (0.90 and 0.50), and the ranking of the concepts is stable across resamples where feature level rankings are not. The regression tutorial shows both on a problem with a known structure, and the study repository reports them on fifteen public benchmarks and four open access datasets.

docs.title: The pool of feature level attributions
sparc.attribution
docs.text:
Feature level Shapley attribution over bootstrap resamples and model classes.

This module implements Steps 1 and 2 of the SPARC algorithm. The reference model is fitted on the training data, the training data is resampled B times, every model class is refitted on every resample, and feature level Shapley values are computed for the instances to be explained with a background sample drawn from the resample. Resample index 0 is always the original training data, so that with B = 1 and M = 1 the pool reduces to the Shapley values of the reference model, which is required for the exact reduction to SHAP.

docs.title: shapley_values
docs.text:
shapley_values(model, X_explain, background, task, explainer='auto', target_class=1, kernel_nsamples='auto', permutation_max_evals='auto', seed=0)

Compute feature level Shapley values for X_explain.

Returns the matrix of Shapley values with shape (n_explain, n_features) and the expected value of the explained output over the background sample. All estimators use the interventional (marginal) expectation with respect to the whole background sample, which is handed to shap as an explicit masker so that no subsampling takes place, and the efficiency property holds with respect to the mean background output. The kernel estimator runs without the l1 feature preselection of shap, so that it targets the full Shapley vector, and it is seeded from seed through the global numpy state, which is restored afterwards, because shap's KernelExplainer draws its coalitions from that state.

docs.title: aggregate_to_concepts
docs.text:
aggregate_to_concepts(values, U)

Equation 1: concept level attribution from feature level attribution.

phi_k = sum_j u_jk phi_j, applied along the last axis of values. Works for pools of shape (..., n_features) and returns (..., n_concepts).

docs.title: redistribute_to_features
docs.text:
redistribute_to_features(concept_values, U, feature_weights=None)

Defuzzified feature level vector from concept centroids.

Each concept value is redistributed to the features in proportion to their membership in the concept: psi_j = sum_k c_k u_jk / sum_j' u_j'k. With feature_weights (one non negative weight per feature, for example the mean absolute feature level attribution of the pool) the share of feature j in concept k is u_jk w_j / sum_j' u_j'k w_j', so that the concept total is unchanged but the credit follows the importance of the members. With an identity membership matrix this returns the concept values unchanged, so the operation reduces to ordinary SHAP for singleton crisp concepts.

docs.title: sparc.concept_shapley
docs.text:
Shapley values computed directly over fuzzy concepts (the direct concept estimator).

The aggregated estimator of Equation 1 forms a concept attribution as the membership weighted sum of feature level Shapley values. The direct estimator of this module treats every fuzzy concept as a player of a cooperative game. A coalition S of concepts keeps feature j to the degree

w_j(S) = min(1, sum_{k in S} u_jk),

the membership mass of j in S, so that the grand coalition keeps every feature entirely whenever the rows of the membership matrix sum to one, and the empty coalition removes every feature. The value of a coalition is the model output of the explained instance with the remaining features removed to the degree 1 - w_j(S), by conditional imputation (mean of the nearest background rows on the kept features, the operation that the deletion and insertion curves of the deletion and insertion tests of the study perform) or by marginal imputation (mean output over the background sample, the interventional expectation of grouped Shapley values). The Shapley value of concept k is the usual weighted average of its marginal contributions; with at most max_exact_concepts concepts every coalition is enumerated, otherwise antithetic permutation sampling is used.

Properties (checked in tests/test_concept_shapley.py):

  • efficiency: the concept values sum to the output of the explained instance minus the value of the empty coalition, for every membership matrix whose rows sum to one;
  • reduction: with the identity membership matrix and marginal imputation the values equal the interventional feature level Shapley values, and with a crisp partition they equal the grouped Shapley values of the baseline;
  • symmetry and duplication invariance follow from the game being defined on the membership mass of a coalition, so that an exact copy of a feature that joins its concept changes no coalition value.

docs.title: sparc.synthetic
docs.text:
Synthetic data generating processes with known concept structure (Phase A).

Three families are implemented. In the additive family the response is a sum of functions of latent factors, each factor being measured by a block of correlated observed features. In the interaction family a product term between the first two factors is added. In the redundancy family exact and near duplicates of features are appended, which produces the credit splitting failure of feature level attribution.

Every latent factor z_k is standard normal and every observed feature of block k is x_j = sqrt(rho) z_k + sqrt(1 - rho) e_j, so that the within block correlation equals rho and every feature is standard normal. Given the block, the factor is normal with mean c_k * sum_j x_j and variance tau_k^2, which gives the true regression function and the true concept attributions in closed form (Gauss Hermite quadrature is used for nonlinear links).

docs.title: sparc.concepts
docs.text:
Fuzzy concept formation from correlated features.

Concepts are formed by fuzzy c means clustering applied to the features rather than to the instances. Every feature is represented by its profile of absolute correlations with all features, so that two features with similar correlation patterns are close, or by a varimax rotated factor analytic loading matrix normalized row wise when a latent structure is assumed. An a priori grouping, for example the subscales of a questionnaire, can be included as an additional candidate partition.

docs.text:

Fuzzy c means clustering of the rows of Z.

Returns the membership matrix U of shape (n_rows, n_clusters) whose rows sum to one, the cluster centers and the final objective value. Several random initializations are run and the solution with the smallest objective is kept. Clusters are ordered by the index of their first dominant row so that the output is deterministic for a given seed. The membership update is written in terms of the ratio of every squared distance to the smallest squared distance in its row, which is the same update algebraically but stays finite for fuzzifier values close to one.

The loadings are therefore varimax rotated, which selects the representative with the simplest structure and makes the membership matrix well defined.

docs.title: sparc.fuzzification
docs.text:
Fuzzification of attribution distributions.

The concept attributions obtained across resamples and model classes form an empirical distribution which is summarized by a trapezoidal fuzzy number whose support is given by the 5th and 95th percentiles and whose core by the 25th and 75th percentiles (Equation 2). Sign confidence, the disagreement index between model classes, interval type 2 upgrades, linguistic labels through the fuzzy compatibility measure (Equation 3), and the possibility degree used for fuzzy ranking are implemented here.

docs.text: Trapezoidal fuzzy number with support [a, d] and core [b, c].

docs.title: centroid
docs.text:
centroid()

Centroid of the trapezoid, always inside the support [a, d].

The closed form is evaluated after translating the trapezoid to its left endpoint a, which avoids the catastrophic cancellation of the raw formula when the four parameters are nearly equal but far from zero, as happens when pool members coincide up to floating point noise. A degenerate (crisp) number returns its single value.

docs.title: sparc.plots
docs.text:
Plots of SPARC explanations.

Every function takes an :class:sparc.Explanation (or a subset of one, explanation[i]), draws with matplotlib on the given or a new axes and returns the axes; show=True calls plt.show(). The plots follow the conventions that users of attribution libraries know, at the concept level:

bar mean absolute attribution of every concept, or the signed attribution of one instance, with the support of the fuzzy number as a whisker; waterfall from the base value to the model output of one instance, concept by concept; beeswarm one row per concept, one dot per instance, coloured by the concept score of the instance; heatmap instances by concepts, instances ordered by the model output; dependence attribution of a concept against its concept score, coloured by the concept with the strongest interaction; force the contributions of one instance pushing the output away from the base value; decision the cumulative path of every instance from the base value to its output through the concepts.

The views that only SPARC can draw:

interval_bars point, core and support of every attribution with the sign confidence and the model class disagreement; linguistic_profile the degree of every linguistic label per concept; disagreement the attribution distribution of every model class; concept_graph the fuzzy partition as a picture of the features; front the Pareto front with the knee, the fidelity optimal member and the current explanation; front_navigator the explanation along the front, member by member; selection_membership how often the front retains every concept and feature; coverage coverage of a replicated attribution by the intervals.

fuzzy_attribution, linguistic_bars, pareto_front and membership of :mod:sparc.plotting are re-exported here.

docs.title: sparc.selection
docs.text:
Multiobjective selection of the explanation configuration.

An explanation configuration consists of the number of concepts K, the fuzzifier exponent, the sparsity level (number of concepts retained after the alpha cut) and the alpha level of the cut. Every candidate is scored on three objectives (Equation 4): fidelity loss of a surrogate fitted on the retained concept attributions and evaluated out of sample, complexity as the number of retained concepts weighted by the fuzziness of their memberships, and instability as one minus the mean rank correlation of concept importance across the pool. The Pareto front is obtained by exhaustive evaluation on a grid or by NSGA II, a default solution is selected by a knee point criterion, and the selection based membership of every concept (Section 3.5), the proportion of distinct Pareto optimal explanations in which it is retained, is derived from the front together with a feature level counterpart.

docs.title: run_nsga2
docs.text:
run_nsga2(pool_provider, n_concepts_bounds, fuzzifier_options, output, extra_partitions=())

NSGA II over (partition source, K, fuzzifier, sparsity, alpha).

pool_provider(K, fuzzifier, source) must return the PartitionPool of the requested candidate; sources are 'fcm' or one of extra_partitions (for example 'apriori'), whose K and fuzzifier are ignored. The sparsity variable is bounded by the largest number of concepts among all candidate sources, so that an extra partition with more concepts than the upper bound of K can be retained in full; the effective sparsity is clipped to the number of concepts of the partition actually evaluated. Alpha is rounded to three decimals once, and the rounded value is used for the archive key, for the evaluation and for the stored configuration, so that the table, the objectives and an explanation rebuilt from the stored configuration refer to the same alpha. The objectives depend on alpha only through the retained set, so they are computed once per distinct explanation (partition and retained set) and shared by every configuration that produces it.

docs.title: SelectionResult dataclass

table has one row per evaluated configuration with the columns of the configuration, the three objectives, retained, feasible, pareto, representative (the first front row of every distinct explanation) and knee. concept_selection_memberships maps every candidate partition name to the Section 3.5 membership of its concepts.

docs.title: fidelity_loss
docs.text:
fidelity_loss(concept_values, retained, output, surrogate='linear', cv=5, random_state=0)

Out of sample error of a surrogate reproducing the model output from retained concepts.

Returns the cross validated mean squared error divided by the variance of the output, that is one minus the cross validated R squared. When no concept is retained the surrogate is the constant mean and the loss is one. An unknown surrogate is rejected before any evaluation.

docs.title: complexity
docs.text:
complexity(U, retained)

Number of retained concepts weighted by their fuzziness: sum_k (1 + F_k).

docs.title: instability
docs.text:
instability(pool, retained, max_pairs=2000, random_state=0)

One minus the mean pairwise Spearman correlation of concept importance across the pool.

Importance of concept k for pool member p is the mean absolute attribution across instances. With fewer than two retained concepts the ranking is trivially stable and the instability is zero by convention.

docs.title: retained_concepts
docs.text:
retained_concepts(quantiles, global_quantiles, alpha, sparsity)

Apply the alpha cut and the sparsity cap.

A concept is active for an instance when the alpha cut of its fuzzy attribution excludes zero. Concepts active for at least one instance pass the cut. Passing concepts are ranked by the alpha level at which they first become active for some instance (activation_threshold minimized over instances, concepts whose support excludes zero for some instance first), ties are broken by decreasing median global importance and then by concept index, and the first sparsity concepts of that ranking are retained.

The ranking key does not depend on alpha and every concept that passes at a lower alpha level ranks ahead of every concept that enters at a higher level, so for a fixed sparsity the retained set at alpha is a subset of the retained set at any larger alpha. Property 6 of the guide (complexity cannot decrease when alpha increases) therefore holds for every sparsity level and every partition, and not only for the count of retained concepts.

Returns the retained concept indices in rank order, the activity of every concept (fraction of instances for which it is active) and the passing mask.

docs.title: knee_point
docs.text:
knee_point(F, mask=None, method='utopia')

Index of the knee point of a Pareto front.

'utopia' returns the front member closest, after min max normalization across the front, to the ideal point. 'hyperplane' returns the member with the largest distance below the hyperplane through the extreme points of the front (the members minimizing each objective).

docs.title: selection_membership
docs.text:
selection_membership(configs, retained_sets, partitions, mask)

Feature level counterpart of the selection based membership.

For every distinct Pareto optimal explanation (one representative per partition and retained set among the rows selected by mask, see representative_mask) a feature is retained with degree equal to its total membership in the retained concepts; the feature selection membership is the mean of that degree over the distinct explanations and lies in [0, 1]. Counting distinct explanations rather than rows makes the value independent of the alpha grid and of the number of alpha values that an optimizer happens to sample for the same explanation.

This is a feature level derived quantity and not the concept membership of Section 3.5 of the guide, which is computed by concept_selection_membership_on_front.

docs.title: concept_selection_membership
docs.text:
concept_selection_membership(U, feature_membership)

Membership weighted average of feature selection memberships per concept.

This maps the feature level quantity of selection_membership back to the concepts of a partition U. For a fuzzy partition the round trip through U mixes concepts, so the result equals the Section 3.5 membership only when U is crisp; the Section 3.5 membership of every candidate partition is computed directly on the front by concept_selection_membership_on_front and stored in SelectionResult.concept_selection_memberships, which is the value to report.

docs.title: Binary classification with known feature groups
docs.text:
The script of this tutorial is examples/classification_breast_cancer.py.

The Wisconsin breast cancer data distributed with scikit-learn has 569 instances and 30 features: ten characteristics of the cell nuclei, each measured as a mean, a standard error and a worst value. The three measurements of one characteristic are strongly correlated, so the data has ten natural groups, and the question for an explanation method is whether it attributes the diagnosis to characteristics rather than splitting the credit among three copies of the same information.

docs.title: Known groups as a candidate partition
docs.text:
data = load_breast_cancer()
X, y, names = data.data, data.target, [n.replace(" ", "_") for n in data.feature_names]
# the a priori groups: the ten characteristics, each measured as mean, error and worst
groups = {}
for j, n in enumerate(names):
    key = n.replace("mean_", "").replace("worst_", "").replace("_error", "")
    groups.setdefault(key, []).append(j)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)

explainer = sparc.Explainer(
    n_resamples=20,
    n_concepts_grid=(2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
    apriori_groups=groups,          # domain knowledge enters as a candidate partition
    partition_source="both",
    target_class=0,                 # classes_ are [0, 1] with 0 = malignant in this dataset
    random_state=0,
    n_jobs=4,
)
explainer.fit(X_train, y_train, feature_names=names)
explanation = explainer(X_test[:80])
print(explanation)
print("explained class:", explanation.attribution.explained_class, "of", explanation.attribution.classes)
print(explanation.describe(0))

Two things are new compared with the regression tutorial. apriori_groups hands the ten characteristics to the explainer as a candidate partition, which competes on the front with the data driven partitions of two to six concepts (partition_source="both"). target_class=0 says which class probability is explained; the classes of the fitted explainer are in explanation.attribution.classes and the explained one in explanation.attribution.explained_class.

docs.title: The partition the data suggest

save(plots.bar(explanation), "bar")
save(plots.membership(explanation.partition), "membership")
save(plots.concept_graph(explanation, min_correlation=0.6), "concept_graph")
save(plots.beeswarm(explanation), "beeswarm")
save(plots.waterfall(explanation[0]), "waterfall")
save(plots.interval_bars(explanation[0]), "interval_bars")

save(plots.selection_membership(explanation), "selection_membership")

The data driven partition is much coarser than the ten characteristics. One concept gathers the size and shape measurements (radius, perimeter, area, concavity and concave points, as means and as worst values), the other texture, smoothness, symmetry, fractal dimension and most of the standard errors. The a priori partition with ten groups is on the front too (the member with K=10 at the top left of the front plot), but it reproduces the model output worse with one retained group, and the knee prefers the two concept partition, which retains one concept, the size and shape one.

docs.title: More than two classes
docs.text:
The script of this tutorial is examples/multiclass_wine.py.

SPARC explains a scalar model output. For a classifier that output is the predicted probability of one class, so a problem with several classes is explained one class at a time, with target_class naming the class. The wine recognition data of scikit-learn (178 instances, 13 features, 3 cultivars) serves as the example.

data = load_wine()
X, y, names = data.data, data.target, list(data.feature_names)
classes = list(data.target_names)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=0)

explanations = {}
for k, class_name in enumerate(classes):
    explainer = sparc.Explainer(n_resamples=20, n_concepts_grid=(2, 3, 4, 5), target_class=k, random_state=0, n_jobs=4)
    explainer.fit(X_train, y_train, feature_names=names)
    explanations[class_name] = explainer(X_test[:40])
    print(class_name, explanations[class_name])

Every explainer trains the same kind of pool on the same data and differs only in the class whose probability is explained; the concept partitions are formed from the features alone, so the three explanations share the same candidate partitions and can be read side by side.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(9, 8.5))
for ax, (class_name, e) in zip(axes, explanations.items()):
    plots.bar(e, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"probability of class {class_name}", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(out / "bar_by_class.png", dpi=120)
plt.close("all")

# one instance, three classes: which concepts push each class probability
i = 0
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(9, 8.5))
for ax, (class_name, e) in zip(axes, explanations.items()):
    plots.interval_bars(e[i], ax=ax, compact=True)
    ax.set_title(f"instance {i}, P({class_name}) = {e.output[i]:.2f}", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(out / "instance_by_class.png", dpi=120)
plt.close("all")

e = explanations[classes[0]]
save(plots.membership(e.partition), "membership")
save(plots.linguistic_profile(e[i]), "linguistic_profile")
save(plots.heatmap(e), "heatmap")

docs.title: One instance, three class probabilities
docs.text: The same wine, explained for every class. The concepts that raise the probability of its class lower the probabilities of the others, and the sign confidence tells how reliably.

docs.title: The partition and the labels
docs.text:
Gradient boosting with several classes

A scikit-learn gradient boosting classifier with more than two classes is explained with the permutation estimator rather than the exact tree estimator, which is slower. Random forests and histogram gradient boosting are explained exactly for any number of classes.

docs.title: Regression with a known concept structure
docs.text:
The script of this tutorial is examples/regression_synthetic.py; every figure below is produced by it.

The problem has three latent factors, each measured by three features that correlate at 0.8 within the block, and a nonlinear response. The true concepts are the three blocks, so the recovered partition, the stability of the ranking and the calibration of the intervals can all be checked.

docs.title: Data and explainer
docs.text:
problem = make_synthetic("additive", n_samples=800, n_features=9, rho=0.8, n_factors=3, random_state=0)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(problem.X, problem.y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
feature_names = [f"x{j}" for j in range(9)]

explainer = sparc.Explainer(n_resamples=20, n_concepts_grid=(2, 3, 4, 5), random_state=0, n_jobs=4)
explainer.fit(X_train, y_train, feature_names=feature_names)
explanation = explainer(X_test[:60])
print(explanation)
print(explanation.describe(0))

The explainer prints its summary and the sentence form of the first instance. The knee explanation here has three concepts, one per block, and retains two of them.

docs.title: Which concepts matter, over all instances and for one
docs.text: The global bar shows the mean absolute attribution of every concept with the support of its fuzzy global importance; the asterisk marks the concepts the knee retains. The beeswarm shows the same per instance, coloured by the concept score of the instance.

docs.title: One instance, with its uncertainty
docs.text: The waterfall walks from the base value to the model output concept by concept. The interval bars add what a point estimate hides: the core and the support of every attribution, its sign confidence and the disagreement between model classes. The fuzzy attribution plot draws the membership functions themselves; where the model classes disagree beyond the threshold the attribution is of type 2 and the band between the model classes is shown.

docs.title: Words, and where they come from
docs.text: The linguistic profile is the compatibility of every label with every concept's fuzzy number; the best label is what describe reports. The disagreement plot shows the resamples of every model class separately, which is where the disagreement index comes from.

docs.title: The concepts
docs.text: The membership heat map and the concept graph show the fuzzy partition: three blocks, recovered from the correlation profiles alone.

docs.title: The front
docs.text: The knee is a default, not a limit. The front plot shows every evaluated configuration, the Pareto front, the knee and the fidelity optimal member; the navigator shows the same instance explained at three members of the front, from the sparsest to the most faithful. The selection membership tells how often the front retains every concept and every feature, a robustness that no single explanation can show.

docs.title: The familiar views
docs.text: Heat map of instances by concepts, dependence of a concept's attribution on its score, force plot and decision plot of the whole sample.

docs.title: Are the intervals honest?
docs.text:
A replicate attribution, the same instances explained by an explainer fitted on another split of the data, should fall inside the support about 90 percent of the time and inside the core about 50 percent of the time.

# a replicate: the same instances explained by an explainer fitted on another split, scored against the intervals
X_train2, _, y_train2, _ = train_test_split(problem.X, problem.y, test_size=0.25, random_state=1)
replica = sparc.Explainer(n_resamples=20, n_concepts_grid=(2, 3, 4, 5), random_state=1, n_jobs=4).fit(X_train2, y_train2, feature_names=feature_names)
replicate = replica(X_test[:60]).feature_attribution()
save(plots.coverage(explanation, replicate), "coverage")

docs.title: Tables and checks
docs.text:
print(explanation.instance_frame(0).round(3).to_string(index=False))
print(explanation.global_frame().round(3).to_string(index=False))
print(explanation.front[["n_concepts", "fuzzifier", "sparsity", "alpha", "fidelity_loss", "complexity", "instability", "knee"]].round(3).to_string())

# the true concept structure is known here: compare the recovered partition with it
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score  # noqa: E402

print("adjusted Rand index of the hardened partition with the true blocks:", round(adjusted_rand_score(problem.true_membership.argmax(axis=1), explanation.partition.labels), 3))
print("sum of concept values + base value = model output:", np.allclose(explanation.values.sum(axis=1) + explanation.base_values, explanation.output, atol=1e-6))

The last two lines verify two things that hold by construction: the concept values plus the base value reproduce the model output of every instance, and the hardened partition is compared with the true blocks by the adjusted Rand index.
